cells.tense: You are at ease acting on a partly-formed impression, right now, in the middle of things.
cells.ask: Take one impression you've been sitting on this week and say it to the person it concerns — plainly, without a case built behind it. Let what they say next be the next thing you take in.
cells.core:
You can move on a half-formed read, and you do. Something comes to you and it matters, well before you could lay out the reasoning — and you don't force the reasoning, which is what keeps it clean. A lot of people panic at not knowing and start assembling an argument; you can stay in the gap a while and let the shape settle.

The thing to watch is what you build on top of the read. Structure laid over a true impression helps everybody in the room; structure that outruns the impression turns into a frame with nothing in it. Hand the read over as a read, and the shape around it stays honest.
cells.sheetLine: You can act on a read you can't yet explain.
cells.verb: reading what matters before you can say why
cells.place: at the seed of it, where nothing shows yet

cells.tense: You will keep gathering and comparing, holding out for a certainty that keeps not arriving.
cells.ask: Choose the question you've been circling longest and pick a day this week to move on the answer you already have. Move first. Let the gathered material sit as notes rather than a gate.
cells.core:
You are treating knowing as something you get by collecting. Another angle, another source, one more pass — the pile grows and the call does not get easier. There's a day you're waiting toward where it finally locks into certainty, and you keep postponing on the strength of it. What you already see gets buried under what you keep adding.

What's needed isn't a cleaner pile. It's a direction you'd steer by, taken before you're finished, and let the sign of whether it's real be that what you've actually developed starts to show on its own — not that every last fact is in. When the direction is live, the next step is clear, and the comparing stops.
cells.sheetLine: You have your answer and you keep asking again.
cells.verb: reading what matters before you can say why

cells.tense: You were thrown off your own perception a while back and are still waiting for someone else to confirm what you see.
cells.ask: Next time you're about to ask someone whether your read is right, stop, write your own view first, then compare. One week of that is the whole practice.
cells.core:
Check with others first, and the checking comes back as the verdict. You look around to find out what you think. What comes to you still arrives — it just doesn't get counted as evidence. The read is there; the standing to use it isn't.

So don't push for certainty — that's not the lever. What recharges this is stepping into the unclear situation with only as much light as you've got, without waiting for the whole road to show, and then doing it again. Each step taken on partial vision rebuilds the trust by showing you the read was carrying you.
cells.sheetLine: Write what you think before you check anyone.

cells.tense: You are moving on a read and filing it under instinct or chance.
cells.ask: Take one decision you've put down to luck and write a sentence naming the impression that was actually steering it. Keep the sentence where you'll run into it.
cells.core:
It's already working. Reads are landing and steering real choices — you notice afterward that the timing was better than it should have been and chalk it up to gut feel or a lucky break. Nothing is missing from the read itself. What's missing is the signing of it, the moment where a name gets put to what was seen.

What's out of balance is the accounting. Your own sense of what's right gets held at arm's length, as if claiming it were vanity, and it comes back out as decisions you can't account for. Name it once. Not a speech — just this is what came to you, and this is why you moved on it.
cells.sheetLine: One thing you called luck was actually your read.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's perceptions 'prove accurate' in any checkable way — the record asserts this, but no one could verify it, so I won't lean on it. The reader might reasonably say the knowing they trust is actually borrowed from someone else or built slowly from experience, not the instant kind described here; the read still holds if so, because the ask is about testing one perception, not about the origin. The ask survives a wrong read because it produces information either way. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line claiming the perceptions 'land without argument' — cut it, and everything here is offered as a trial.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that what the person senses proves out — the record says so, but no outside test confirms it, so nothing here should rest on that being true. A reader could fairly say what they call a read is really a slow build from experience or something picked up from someone else, and the ask still works either way, because testing one impression returns information whatever its origin. The line that serves me more than the person is any version of 'your perceptions land,' which flatters the card instead of offering them something to try.
